job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Lena Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake up late-ish, because I work in the evenings when my head's clearest. Mornings are for applications and a bit of freelance work, building dashboards for a friend's ceramics shop. I share a flat in Aarhus with two flatmates, Mette and Jonas, and we cook together most nights. I finished a marketing and business analytics degree in June with top marks, plus internships at a meal-kit start-up and a retail chain's analytics team, and I'm now looking for the right first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and also a bit boring. I use AI tools every day, so I know where they help and where they don't. I'd tell my friends it's a nice assistant, and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel fine. My work is already half-automated by the tools I use, and the market round here is wide open. I don't see a threat. The real question is which job gives me the best learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd apply to about six places a week and keep the freelance work going, because it's a real portfolio. I'd also finish the online course on causal analysis I started in September. And I'd save a bit, since I have over six months already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'm excited, honestly. I'm 23, I've got a good degree and the tools, and no debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one pressure in your life right now that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The honest one is that I want a job that isn't just spreadsheets. The ceramics shop work is the first time I've seen what I made change what someone sold. I want more of that, and I worry a big firm would put me in a corner doing reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you talk to about the job search, and what would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mette, who works in a bank's marketing team, and my old internship manager Karsten. Mette says choose the team, not the brand. Karsten says to show a dashboard I built, not to describe one. Both of those are right, and I do it.

say: I'd say AI is a **nice assistant** and nothing more.
I'd show friends the **dashboards** I build rather than talk about them.
think: My work is already **half-automated** by tools I use daily, so I see no threat.
The real question is which job gives me the **best learning**.
do: Apply to **six places a week** and keep my freelance dashboard work going.
Finish the online course on **causal analysis**.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, with a good degree, the tools and no debt.
S0.quote: I'm 23, I've got a good degree and the tools, and no debt.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** makes her see the technology as a tool, not a threat.
What worries her is the quality of the first job, not whether one exists.
Freelance dashboards give her a real portfolio and a second path.

steps.text: Apply to six teams a week, choosing the team over the brand
Finish the online course on causal analysis
Keep building dashboards for the ceramics shop and other small firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming and we should get good at it. At work I'd say the people who learn the tools win. Online I'd actually post about it, with examples from my freelance work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means many analyst jobs change. The basic reporting I did in my internship is already done by the tools, and a junior just checks it. So the entry-level job becomes a job about judgment, and firms might want fewer of us. I'm fine, because I'm good at the judgment part, but I know friends who aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean in. I'd make my freelance work into a small business, with three or four steady clients, and use it as a safety net while I take a job. I'd learn automation properly, so I can build workflows for small shops that can't afford a data team. And I'd pay into a union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. There's some friction, because the first job might be strange, but there's also a lot of room. I like change, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry-level tasks in your field would go first, and what does that do to a job like the one you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for a mixed route. A job at a company with an analytics team, plus the side business. I'd push for fair rules on how firms treat the people whose tasks they automate, because I'd hate being fine while friends are not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who graduated a year after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the people who thrive aren't the ones with the best marks, they're the ones who ask good questions and aren't afraid of the tools. I'd show them how to do a first project with a free tool this weekend. Then I'd tell them to keep one human skill, like talking to clients.

say: I'd say the people who **learn the tools** win, and post examples online.
I'd call for **fair rules** on how firms treat people whose tasks are automated.
think: The routine reporting I did is already done by tools, so entry jobs become about **judgment**.
do: Grow my freelance work into three or four **steady clients**.
Learn **automation** well enough to build workflows for small shops.
feel: Pretty **calm**: some friction, but a lot of room, and I like change.
S1.quote: The people who thrive aren't the ones with the best marks, they're the ones who ask good questions and aren't afraid of the tools.
fieldNote: Her adaptability keeps her **calm**: she expects the change to open work for her.
Progressive politics show up as concern for friends who adapt less easily.
Builds a **side business** as a safety net while taking a job.

steps.text: Turn freelance dashboard work into three or four steady small-shop clients
Learn workflow automation to build tools for small shops
Take an analytics job with a team that trains juniors
Join a union and back fair rules for automated workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and I'd say it clearly. Governments, schools, my own generation. I'd post long threads, and I'd write to my MP, because two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel scared. If the AI I use every day becomes as good as a graduate, a company has no reason to hire graduates at all. I know the tools better than most people my age, and I'd still be unsure what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever job I can get now and put my savings to work. I'd put most of the freelance effort into the one thing machines can't do easily: talking to people who are scared of the change, helping small shops adjust. I'd also go to the first public meeting on support schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also curious. It's frightening and it's the biggest story of my life. I'd be buzzing and sick at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about how you spend the next few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next months turn into building relationships. I'd call every client and every old manager, and tell them I can help them adapt. I think trust will matter more than skill when the skill is free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family the night this was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents I'm okay because I have a cushion and I'm not scared of the tools. I'd also say I want to use this to help other people get through, not only myself. I wouldn't say how sick I feel.

say: I'd say **we're not ready** and write to my MP.
I'd post **long threads** online because two years is nothing.
think: If the AI I use every day matches a graduate, firms have **no reason** to hire graduates.
I know the tools well and still wonder **what I'm for**.
do: Take **any decent job** now and put savings to work.
Call every **client and old manager** and offer help adapting.
feel: **Anxious** and curious: frightening and the biggest story of my life.
S2.quote: I know the tools better than most people my age, and I'd still be unsure what I'm for.
fieldNote: Her comfort with tools doesn't remove the fear; she asks what a **graduate is for**.
Her plan is relationships and trust, not more technical skill.
Admits she'd hide how **sick** she feels from her parents.

steps.text: Take any decent job within two months to have an income
Call every client and old manager to offer help with adapting
Write to her MP and attend the first support scheme meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a deadline, and a useful one. Five years is long enough to build something if you start now. I'd say that at dinner, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my twenties are the window. I'd work hard now, get a cushion, and build a little business that won't rely on a job. I'd feel like I have just enough time to turn into someone who isn't a junior anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take a job where I'm close to clients and decisions. Build the freelance business to six clients by year two. Save about 40 percent of my pay. And take a short course in coaching or facilitation, because I want a skill about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. I feel pushed, like a deadline, not like a threat. That's the better kind of stress, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is scramble, five is build. I'd set up a small limited company for the freelance work and treat it seriously, with a bookkeeper. With two years I'd have skipped the company and just taken whatever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, or start doing, that you wouldn't if it were sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating a company as a ladder I climb. I'd treat it as a place to learn and then leave. And I'd start thinking about what I'd want to do if money was no problem, because that might become a real question.

say: I'd say five years is a **useful deadline** if you start now.
I'd tell friends to treat their **twenties** as the window.
think: My twenties are the window to build a cushion and a **small business**.
I want to stop being a **junior anything**.
do: Take a job close to **clients and decisions**.
Grow the freelance work to **six clients** and save about 40 percent.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way: pushed like a deadline, not threatened.
S3.quote: I'd stop treating a company as a ladder I climb. I'd treat it as a place to learn and then leave.
fieldNote: Five years push her to turn **freelancing** into a proper business.
Wants a people skill such as coaching, to pair with her tool skills.
Treats employers as stepping stones, a sharp break from the usual graduate path.

steps.text: Take a job close to clients and decisions
Grow freelance work to six steady clients by year two
Save about 40 percent of every payslip
Take a short course in coaching and facilitation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best-case version of a hard problem. There's time for schools to change and for people to retrain. I'd say we should stop arguing and start building, and I'd offer to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good. Ten years is a full career's start. I'd be 33, with a business or two, a decent pile saved, and the tools I know. I'd just have to not get lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Join a firm for two or three years, learn how it works, then go out on my own with the freelance business. I'd buy a small flat. I'd also help teach a free evening class in analytics at the library, because the more people who learn it, the more I'll learn too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite excited. This is the version that feels like an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big thing would be using the time. I'd run small experiments, like trying to automate a client's entire monthly reporting, and see what breaks. If I'm good at it, that's a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you feel safe, or does it just push the worry further off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade feels safe for me, personally. But I'd still feel it for people who don't have my cushion or my habit of trying tools, and I'd like to help them. If I'm honest, the worry is that nothing will be done until it's too late.

say: I'd say it's the **best-case** version of a hard problem.
I'd offer to **help** schools and people retrain.
think: At 33 I'd have a **business or two**, savings and the tools.
I'd just have to **not get lazy**.
do: Join a firm for two or three years, then go **out on my own**.
Teach a free **analytics class** at the library.
feel: **Calm** and excited: this one feels like an opportunity.
S4.quote: I'd run small experiments, like trying to automate a client's entire monthly reporting, and see what breaks.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees a **real opportunity** and plans a business.
Her only worry is that nothing will be done for **others** until too late.
Her idea of teaching a library class links her ease to community.

steps.text: Join a firm for two or three years to learn how it works
Automate a client's monthly reporting as a test project
Teach a free evening analytics class at the library
Buy a small flat from steady monthly savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, even though I'd cope better than most. It's the speed that scares me, and the feeling that nobody's in charge. What would help is retraining that's paid for, honest numbers from firms about what they'll automate, and some kind of income floor. And people who show others the tools without making them feel stupid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that people think I'm optimistic because I'm good with tools. It's more that I have a safety net, and I know it. If I didn't, I'd be asking the same questions as everyone else.

headlineQuote: I have a safety net, and I know it. If I didn't, I'd be asking the same questions as everyone else.
portrait: Lena is 23, a **top graduate** in marketing and business analytics from Aarhus, sharing a flat with two friends.
She uses AI tools every day and sees them as an **assistant**, not a threat.
She builds dashboards for small shops and plans to grow that into a **side business**.
Her mood ranges from calm to anxious, and only the **2028** world truly shakes her.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because speed and a lack of anyone in charge scare her.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining**, honest numbers from firms, an income floor, and people who teach the tools kindly.
